h1: Video that ranks on YouTube and on Google
metaTitle: YouTube SEO Services for Indian Channels and Brands
metaDescription: YouTube SEO aimed at Google video results as well as YouTube search, with chapters, transcripts and Hindi metadata. From ₹30,000 a month, ex-GST.
answer: YouTube SEO means making your videos findable in two places: YouTube's own search and Google's video results. The work is keyword research in both, chapters and clean transcripts, Hindi or bilingual metadata, and embedding the video on the page that already ranks. From ₹30,000 a month, ex-GST.
takeaways: Two rankers, one upload. YouTube search rewards retention; Google's video results reward a page that answers the query and a video it can read.
**Chapters are not decoration.** They're how Google builds key moments, and they're how a nine-minute video gets to answer a two-minute question.
Auto-captions on Indian-accented English and Hinglish are unreliable. A corrected transcript is the cheapest ranking work on the list.
The first 30 seconds decides retention, retention decides distribution, and no amount of tag stuffing outranks that.
Sits inside the Organic Social & Content retainer: ₹30,000 / ₹50,000 / ₹70,000 a month, ex-GST.

body: Almost every "YouTube SEO" package sold in India optimises for one system: YouTube's internal search. That's the smaller of the two opportunities. YouTube search is dominated by browse and suggested traffic, and it rewards signals you mostly earn after publishing — click-through on the thumbnail, how long people stay, whether they watch another one.

Google's video results are a different animal. When somebody searches a how-to, a demo, an unboxing or a "how much does X cost in India" query, Google can return a video block near the top of the page. Getting into it is closer to ordinary [SEO](/seo) than to channel growth: the query has to genuinely warrant video, the video has to be crawlable and readable, and a page that Google already trusts is a strong place to host it.

So we plan every video as one asset with two jobs. The metadata, chapters and transcript serve Google. The packaging and the first 30 seconds serve YouTube. Neither set of work costs the other anything, which is the whole reason this is worth doing properly rather than uploading and hoping.

sections.h2: Keyword research: YouTube's suggest is not Google's index
body: Search demand on YouTube and search demand on Google overlap far less than people assume. "GST filing" on Google is a lot of people looking for a portal. On YouTube it's a lot of people looking for someone to walk them through the screen. Researching one and publishing for the other is the most common reason a channel gets views but no business.

callout.title: The query test
callout.body: Before we script anything, we run the query in Google and look. If there's no video block and no strong intent to watch something, video is the wrong format for that keyword and a written page will beat it for a tenth of the cost. We'll say so.

sections.h2: The machine-readable layer: chapters, transcripts, captions, Hindi
body: This is the part that gets skipped, and it's the part that makes a video eligible for anything on Google. A video with no chapters and a garbled auto-transcript is, to a crawler, nine minutes of nothing.
bullets: **Chapters**, following YouTube's rules: the first timestamp starts at 00:00, at least three chapters, none shorter than ten seconds. Written as answers, not as "Intro / Part 1 / Outro", because those labels are what Google can show as key moments.

**A corrected transcript.** Auto-captions on Indian-accented English, and on any Hinglish at all, produce reliable nonsense around exactly the words that matter — product names, place names, numbers. We fix it and upload it as a caption file.

**A second-language caption track** where the audience warrants it. Hindi subtitles on an English video, or English on a Hindi one, cost very little and widen the searchable text considerably. YouTube also supports multi-language audio tracks if you have the source files.
**Descriptions written for a reader**, not a keyword counter. First two lines carry the answer and the link, timestamps sit below, and there's no wall of comma-separated phrases at the bottom.
**Tags matter far less than the industry claims.** They help with spelling variants and brand misspellings. That's roughly it.
**Bilingual metadata where the search term genuinely is bilingual.** People search "GST return kaise file kare" in Roman script, and titling it in formal Hindi misses them entirely.

sections.h2: Titles, thumbnails and the first 30 seconds
body: On YouTube itself, distribution is bought with two numbers: how many people click, and how many stay. Everything else is downstream of those.

The thumbnail and title work as a pair, which means testing them as a pair — YouTube's built-in thumbnail test tool does this natively now, and it's more honest than an argument in a review call. Our rule is that the thumbnail carries the situation and the title carries the promise. If they say the same thing twice, one of them is wasted.

Then the first 30 seconds. Most brand videos spend them on a logo animation and a greeting, which is where the retention graph falls off a cliff you can see from the analytics tab. Open by restating the exact query the viewer typed, say what they'll have by the end, then start. Save the introductions for people who already subscribed.
None of this is a growth hack, and we don't sell it as one. It's the difference between a video that gets recommended and a video that sits at 240 views with excellent tags.

callout.title: Bought views are worse than no views
callout.body: Purchased views and engagement break the retention data YouTube uses to decide who else sees the video, and they violate YouTube's own policies on fake engagement. You end up paying to teach the algorithm that nobody watches your content.

sections.h2: Embedding video where your pages already rank
body: The multiplier nobody uses: put the video on the page that's already ranking for the query, with proper markup, and one upload works twice.

Practically that means a video gets a home on your site — an existing service or answer page where it belongs, not a dumping-ground /videos directory. The embed is accompanied by the transcript in text, so the page carries the words even for people who won't press play, and [VideoObject schema](/services/schema-markup-services) tells Google what the video is, how long it is and where the key moments sit.

The two channels then feed each other. The page gives the video a crawlable, trusted host. The video gives the page something the text-only competitors don't have, and a reason for a visitor to stay on it. For anything demo-shaped or how-to-shaped, this is usually a bigger win than another month of chasing subscribers.

sections.h2: The baseline we freeze on video, and what the guarantee says
body: Two numbers get frozen at kickoff, from the trailing 90 days: views arriving from YouTube search and Google search — not browse, not suggested, not external — and organic sessions to the pages that host your videos. Those are the numbers video work is judged on, because they're the ones that respond to optimisation rather than to luck or to a post going wide.

Suggested and browse traffic gets reported too, and it's frequently the bigger number. We just don't claim credit for it. Recommendation traffic is driven by the content being good and by YouTube deciding to push it, and dressing that up as an SEO result would be dishonest.

The company guarantee runs as it does on every other retainer: your trailing-90-day qualified leads from organic search are frozen on day one, and if we haven't beaten that in 90 days we keep working free until we do. We never promise a ranking position, on Google or in YouTube search — nobody controls either index. If video is one input among several, we'll say plainly which part of the movement we think it caused and how confident we are. How we report all of this is set out on the [SEO reporting page](/services/seo-reporting-services).

faqs.q: How much do YouTube SEO services cost in India?
faqs.a: Ours sit in the Organic Social & Content retainer at ₹30,000, ₹50,000 or ₹70,000 a month, ex-GST, depending on publishing volume and whether the back catalogue needs work. Cheaper packages around ₹10,000 a month usually mean title and tag edits from a template, which is a tool's job.

faqs.q: Does YouTube SEO help my website rank on Google?
faqs.a: Indirectly, and only if you host the video properly. Embedding it on the page targeting that query, with the transcript in text and VideoObject schema, gives that page something text-only competitors lack. A video sitting only on YouTube helps YouTube.

faqs.q: Do tags still matter on YouTube?
faqs.a: Much less than the industry sells. YouTube has said tags play a minimal role, mainly helping with misspellings and spelling variants. Titles, thumbnails, the first 30 seconds and the transcript do the real work. If someone's package is mostly tag research, you're paying for the least useful part.

faqs.q: Should our videos be in Hindi or English?
faqs.a: Check how the query is actually typed. A lot of Indian search demand is Hinglish in Roman script — "kaise kare" written in English letters — and neither pure English nor formal Hindi metadata catches it. Often the right answer is one language of audio with the other as captions.

faqs.q: How long before YouTube SEO shows results?
faqs.a: Faster than site SEO in one direction and slower in another. Re-titling and re-chaptering an existing video with views can move within two to four weeks. Building search-sourced views on a new channel takes three to six months, because YouTube needs data before it will distribute anything widely.

faqs.q: Can you guarantee my video will rank first on YouTube?
faqs.a: No. YouTube results are personalised by watch history, so there isn't one fixed ranking to promise. What we commit to is movement against your own frozen baseline of search-sourced views and organic sessions to video pages, measured over 90 days.
